title: Length-Weighted Loss Does Not Explain the Repetition Advantage in Long-CoT Supervised Fine-Tuning

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution tests the hypothesis that the Long-CoT "repetition advantage" arises because per-sequence mean cross-entropy loss underweights long reasoning traces. Paper [15] ("Data Repetition Beats Data Scaling in Long-CoT Supervised Fine-Tuning") investigates the repetition advantage in Long-CoT fine-tuning but attributes it to data repetition rather than loss weighting. No prior paper explicitly establishes or tests the hypothesis that mean cross-entropy loss underweights long reasoning traces. Thus, the purpose is **NONE**.

### Mechanism
The mechanism introduces a length-weighted loss \( L_{\text{len}} = (T/T_{\text{ref}}) \cdot L_{\text{mean}} \), which upweights long sequences proportionally. Paper [7] ("Clip Your Sequences Fairly") addresses length bias in sequence-level RL by introducing length-fair clipping, which adjusts optimization weights based on sequence length. Paper [14] ("Rethinking the Comparison Unit in Sequence-Level Reinforcement Learning") also discusses length-related loss scaling but frames the issue as a comparison unit problem rather than introducing a proportional length-weighted loss. Paper [27] ("Correcting Length Bias in Neural Machine Translation") applies per-word rewards to address length bias in NMT, which is conceptually similar to upweighting longer sequences. These papers collectively cover the mechanism at the primitive level (adjusting loss weights based on sequence length). Thus, the mechanism is **COVERED**.

### Evaluation
The evaluation uses AIME and GPQA benchmarks to compare length-weighted loss against standard data scaling, measuring accuracy and recovery of the repetition advantage gap. Paper [15] ("Data Repetition Beats Data Scaling in Long-CoT Supervised Fine-Tuning") uses the same benchmarks (AIME and GPQA) to evaluate Long-CoT fine-tuning strategies, including repetition and data scaling. The evaluation design (benchmark family and metric semantics) is identical, even though the specific comparison (length-weighted loss vs. standard scaling) differs. Thus, the evaluation is **COVERED**.

### Domain
The domain is Long chain-of-thought supervised fine-tuning of LLMs. Papers [2], [5], [9], [15], and [12] all address Long-CoT reasoning or fine-tuning in LLMs, covering the same general application area. Thus, the domain is **COVERED**.

### Purpose
The contribution aims to redirect the explanation of the repetition advantage away from gradient signal distribution. None of the prior papers explicitly report or establish the same empirical relationship — that the repetition advantage is not due to gradient signal distribution but instead points toward memorization convergence through repeated exposure. While several papers discuss memorization (e.g., [5], [6], [10], [24]), none specifically refute gradient signal distribution as the mechanism behind repetition advantage.

### Mechanism
The contribution uses negative results to eliminate gradient-signal-distribution explanations and argues for an alternative mechanism (memorization convergence through repeated exposure). Paper [14] discusses the role of data repetition in Long-CoT SFT and its benefits for generalization, but it does not eliminate gradient signal distribution as an explanation or propose memorization convergence as the mechanism. Paper [4] discusses coherent gradients as an explanation for generalization but does not address repetition advantage or its mechanism. No prior paper uses the same mechanism to refute gradient signal distribution and propose memorization convergence.

### Evaluation
The contribution provides evidence that the mechanism is not gradient signal distribution, pointing toward memorization convergence through repeated exposure (termination rate 90% vs 46%). Paper [14] evaluates the impact of data repetition in Long-CoT SFT, but its evaluation design focuses on generalization performance rather than disproving gradient signal distribution as an explanation. Paper [10] studies repetition in memorization but does not use the same evaluation design to refute gradient signal distribution. No prior paper uses the same evaluation design to validate this specific claim.

### Domain
The contribution operates in the domain of mechanistic analysis of Long-CoT SFT. Paper [1] and paper [14] both address Long-CoT SFT, making the domain covered. While the specific sub-problem (refuting gradient signal distribution) is new, the general application area (Long-CoT SFT) is not.
